nodes.label: eqbocop2

nodes.name: Contagion (financial)
nodes.statement: Contagion, by definition, refers to the idea that any type of financial crisis may spread from one subject (financial institution) to another.
differentia: any type of financial crisis may spread from one subject (financial institution) to another

nodes.name: Contagion transmission with immunity after recovery
nodes.statement: In our work, we assume that contagion can be transmitted from an infected bank to another one, which has not yet been infected, and after recovery the bank produces immunity for a long time.

nodes.name: SIR model
nodes.statement: In order to simulate an epidemiological process of such diseases, there is a well-known suitable model, called SIR, which was first introduced in the works of Kermack and McKendrick \cite{[21]}.

nodes.name: SIR classes S, I, R
nodes.statement: The model is named SIR for the reason that population is divided into three classes: class $S$ of susceptible, those who are susceptible to the disease; class $I$ of infected, those who are ill/infected; class $R$ of recovered, those who are recovered and have become immune to the disease.
nodes.statement_short: Population split into susceptible $S$, infected $I$, recovered $R$ classes.

nodes.name: SIR bank contagion risk model
nodes.statement: The earlier formulated rules of bank transitions from one condition to another lead to the following system of differential equations: \begin{equation} \begin{cases} \displaystyle \frac{dS(t)}{dt} = - \beta S(t) I(t),\\[0.3cm] \displaystyle \frac{dI(t)}{dt} = \beta S(t) I(t) - \gamma I(t),\\[0.3cm] \displaystyle \frac{dR(t)}{dt} = \gamma I(t), \end{cases} \end{equation} $t \in [0,T]$, subject to the initial conditions \begin{equation} S(0) = S_0, \quad I(0) = I_0, \quad R(0) = R_0. \end{equation} The first equation defines the number of banks that leave the group $S$ by becoming a target of market speculation at time $t$; the second equation defines the number of contagious banks at time $t$; and the third equation defines the number of banks that have recovered from the crisis at time $t$, where $t\in [0,T]$, $T > 0$.
nodes.statement_short: SIR ODE system for susceptible, contagious and recovered banks with initial conditions on $[0,T]$.

nodes.name: Contagion spreading rate beta
nodes.statement: Parameter $\beta$ denotes the contagion spreading rate. It represents the strength of contagion, where a susceptible bank, that is in contact with a single infected bank, changes its state to infected with probability $\beta$.

nodes.name: Speed of recovery gamma
nodes.statement: The second parameter, $\gamma$, denotes the speed of recovery. It represents the resistance to contagion. Therefore, an infected bank changes its state to recover with probability $\gamma$.

nodes.name: Homogeneous banks with constant parameters
nodes.statement: According to the standard SIR methodology, we are assuming that all banks are similar, and both parameters $\beta$ and $\gamma$ are constant for the entire sample.

nodes.name: Fixed number of institutions N
nodes.statement: It is assumed that $N$, the number of institutions during the period of time under study, is fixed throughout the contamination time (in our simulations, $N=169$ --- see Section~\ref{s3}). It means that $S(t)+I(t)+R(t) = N$ for all $t\in [0, T]$.
nodes.statement_short: Total number $N$ of banks is constant, so $S+I+R=N$.

nodes.name: Initial condition assumption
nodes.statement: Moreover, we assume that the initial conditions \eqref{eqIC} at the beginning of the period under study satisfy \begin{equation} S(0)\gg I(0)>0 \quad \text{ and } \quad R(0)=0. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Initial values for 169 European banks
nodes.statement: Therefore, using the information that the total number of banking institutions ($N$) is equal to 169, and assuming that only one bank is contagious at the initial time, the values of initial conditions for the SIR model were obtained: $S(0)=168$, $I(0)=1$, and $R(0)=0$.
nodes.section: 3 SIR model simulations with real data

nodes.name: Three contagion scenarios (Portugal, Spain, UK)
nodes.statement: In our work, in order to present contrast scenarios of contagion spreading among European banks, we have chosen three countries that have completely different values of parameters $\beta$ and $\gamma$: \begin{enumerate} \item in the first scenario, the initially contagious bank is located in Portugal; \item in the second scenario, the group $I$ of infected consists only of a bank from Spain; \item while in the third scenario the contamination begins from a United Kingdom's bank. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 3 SIR model simulations with real data
nodes.statement_short: Scenarios 1-3: the initially contagious bank is in Portugal, Spain or the UK.

nodes.name: Contagion dynamics depend on originating country
nodes.statement: In the first scenario, contagion spreads rapidly. In a short span of time, contagion reaches its peak and then swiftly decreases. The recovery process takes fast. See Figure~\ref{f2a}. Regarding the second scenario, Figure~\ref{f2b} demonstrates that contamination occurs rapidly as in the first scenario. The contagion affects a large number of banks but the recovery process takes longer. In Figure~\ref{f2c}, we see what happens in the third scenario: the spread of contagion occurs in a longer period of time and, consequently, the recovery process goes slowly too. The graphs of Figure~\ref{f2} show that the processes of contagion take place in different ways, depending on the country where it begins.
nodes.section: 3 SIR model simulations with real data
conclusions: the processes of contagion take place in different ways, depending on the country where it begins
nodes.statement_short: Simulations over $T=100$ days: fast spread/recovery for Portugal, slower recovery for Spain, slow spread and recovery for UK.

nodes.name: T=100 insufficient for contagion-free equilibrium in scenarios 2 and 3
nodes.statement: Figure~\ref{f2} also shows that, in case of the first scenario, contagion has almost reached the contagion-free equilibrium ($I(T)=0$) at the end of 100 days. However, $T=100$ is not enough to reach the contagion-free equilibrium for the second and third scenarios.
nodes.section: 3 SIR model simulations with real data
conclusions: in case of the first scenario, contagion has almost reached the contagion-free equilibrium ($I(T)=0$) at the end of 100 days
$T=100$ is not enough to reach the contagion-free equilibrium for the second and third scenarios

nodes.name: Time to contagion-free equilibrium per scenario
nodes.statement: As seen from Figure~\ref{f3a}, in case of bank contagion starting in Portugal, less than in half a year the contagion spreading stops. Figure~\ref{f3b} demonstrates that a spreading of contagion starting in Spain will only stop after a full year. The third scenario is the most severe: the contagion will disappear and the banks will be recovered only after three years (see Figure~\ref{f3c}).
nodes.section: 3 SIR model simulations with real data
conclusions: less than in half a year the contagion spreading stops
a spreading of contagion starting in Spain will only stop after a full year
the contagion will disappear and the banks will be recovered only after three years
nodes.statement_short: Contagion dies out in under half a year (Portugal), a year (Spain), three years (UK).

nodes.name: Economic relevance explains scenario differences
nodes.statement: The reason behind the differences found, for the three scenarios considered, rely in the different economic relevance, in the global banking market, of the countries where contagion begins.
nodes.section: 3 SIR model simulations with real data

nodes.name: Optimal control problem for bank contagion (Bolza form)
nodes.statement: Since one of the main goals is to avoid the wide dissemination of a contagion, we pose the following optimal control problem: \begin{equation} \min \mathcal{J}[I(\cdot),u(\cdot)] =I(T)+\int\limits_0^T b u^2(t) dt \longrightarrow \min \end{equation} subject to the control system \begin{equation} \begin{cases} \displaystyle \frac{dS(t)}{dt} = - \beta S(t) I(t),\\[0.3cm] \displaystyle \frac{dI(t)}{dt} = \beta S(t) I(t) - \gamma I(t)-u(t)I(t),\\[0.3cm] \displaystyle \frac{dR(t)}{dt} = \gamma I(t)+u(t)I(t), \end{cases} \end{equation} where $S(0) = S_0$, $I(0) = I_0$, $R(0) = R_0$, satisfying \eqref{eq:IC:assump}, and the weight $b > 0$, are fixed.
nodes.statement_short: Minimize final contagious banks $I(T)$ plus quadratic control cost subject to SIR dynamics with treatment control $u$.

nodes.name: Simulation initial values and weight b=1.5
nodes.statement: In our simulations, the initial values of the state variables are given as discussed in Section~\ref{s3}, while the weight $b$, associated with the cost of control measures, is taken to be $1.5$, motivated by the value of possible recapitalization with state funds considered in \cite{[24]}.

nodes.name: Control u (Central Bank assistance rate)
nodes.statement: The control $u(\cdot)$ is a Lebesgue function with values in the compact set $[0, 1]$: $0 \leq u(t) \leq 1$, with $u(t)$ denoting the rate at which assistance will be provided to contagious banks, that is, it is the ratio between the financial support from the Central Bank at time $t$ and the financial needed by the banks at that time. In this way, $u(t) = 1$ means full support from the Central Bank at time $t$ (all money needed by the banks is being covered by Central Bank), while $u(t) = 0$ means no financial lending or recapitalization from the Central Bank at time $t$.
differentia: with values in the compact set $[0, 1]$
nodes.statement_short: $u(t)\in[0,1]$ is the fraction of banks' needed financial support provided by the Central Bank.

nodes.name: Optimal control problem in Mayer form
nodes.statement: In order to use the \textsf{BOCOP} optimal control solver \cite{[25],Bocop}, the optimal control problem in Bolza form \eqref{eqopt1}--\eqref{eqopt2} is rewritten in the following equivalent Mayer form: \begin{equation} \min \mathcal{J}[S(\cdot),R(\cdot),Y(\cdot)] =N-S(T)-R(T)+Y(T)\longrightarrow \min \end{equation} subject to \begin{equation} \begin{cases} \displaystyle \frac{dS(t)}{dt} = \beta S^2(t)+ \beta S(t)(R(t)-N),\\[0.3cm] \displaystyle \frac{dR(t)}{dt} = \gamma (N-S(t)-R(t))+u(t)(N-S(t)-R(t)),\\[0.3cm] \displaystyle \frac{dY(t)}{dt} = bu^2(t),\\[0.3cm] \displaystyle S(0)=S_0, \quad R(0)=0, \quad Y(0)=0,\\[0.3cm] u(t) \in [0, 1]. \end{cases} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Equivalent Mayer reformulation with $I=N-S-R$ and auxiliary state $Y$ accumulating control cost.

nodes.name: BOCOP direct transcription with Ipopt
nodes.statement: The optimal control problem \eqref{eqbocop1}--\eqref{eqbocop2} is approximated by \textsf{BOCOP} into a nonlinear programming problem (NLP) using a standard time discretization. The NLP problem is then solved by the open-source \textsf{Ipopt} optimization solver \cite{ipopt}, using sparse exact derivatives computed by the \textsf{Adol-C} (Automatic Differentiation by OverLoading in \textsf{C++}) package \cite{ADOL-C}.
nodes.statement_short: Discretize the control problem in time into an NLP with BOCOP, then solve it with Ipopt using ADOL-C exact sparse derivatives.

nodes.name: Time discretization to NLP
nodes.statement: The optimal control problem \eqref{eqbocop1}--\eqref{eqbocop2} is approximated by \textsf{BOCOP} into a nonlinear programming problem (NLP) using a standard time discretization.
nodes.statement_short: Transcribe the control problem into an NLP by time discretization.

nodes.name: Solve NLP with Ipopt
nodes.statement: The NLP problem is then solved by the open-source \textsf{Ipopt} optimization solver \cite{ipopt}, using sparse exact derivatives computed by the \textsf{Adol-C} (Automatic Differentiation by OverLoading in \textsf{C++}) package \cite{ADOL-C}.
nodes.statement_short: Solve the NLP with Ipopt using ADOL-C derivatives.

nodes.name: Optimal control result, scenario 1 (Portugal)
nodes.statement: Figure~\ref{f4a} shows that if we have no interest to stop contagiousness or just do not want to spend any money on it, that is, $u(t) \equiv 0$, then, in case of the first scenario, the number of contagious banks at final time $T=30$ will be equal to 64. If the control $u(t)$ is chosen as the solution of our optimal control problem, then in one month the number of contagious banks will become smaller than $\mathcal{J}=2$, see Figure~\ref{f4b}.
assumptions: in case of the first scenario
conclusions: the number of contagious banks at final time $T=30$ will be equal to 64
in one month the number of contagious banks will become smaller than $\mathcal{J}=2$
nodes.statement_short: Portugal: 64 contagious banks at $T=30$ without control vs fewer than 2 with optimal control.

nodes.name: Optimal control result, scenario 2 (Spain)
nodes.statement: In case of the second scenario, Figure~\ref{f5a} shows that the number of contagious without control is equal to 124. In contrast, the number of contagious banks at time $T=30$ using optimal control, taking into account the costs associated with the control interventions during all the period $[0,30]$, is equal to 2 (see Figure~\ref{f5b}). On the other hand, after one month, the number of banks that already recovered from the risks are less than fifty without control; while with optimal control measures this number is almost double.
assumptions: In case of the second scenario
conclusions: the number of contagious without control is equal to 124
nodes.statement_short: Spain: 124 contagious banks without control vs 2 with optimal control; recovered banks almost double.

nodes.name: Optimal control result, scenario 3 (UK)
nodes.statement: Finally, when the contagion begins from United Kingdom (third scenario), the number of contagious banks at final time $T=30$ is 149 without control (Figure~\ref{f6a}) with that number decreasing to less than 4 when the Central Bank applies optimal control (see Figure~\ref{f6b}).
assumptions: when the contagion begins from United Kingdom (third scenario)
conclusions: the number of contagious banks at final time $T=30$ is 149 without control (Figure~\ref{f6a}) with that number decreasing to less than 4 when the Central Bank applies optimal control
nodes.statement_short: UK: 149 contagious banks without control vs fewer than 4 with optimal control.

nodes.name: Robustness of results to the weight b
nodes.statement: It is worth to mention that the qualitative results of the paper do not change with the particular choice of the weight $b$: the extremal curves change continuously with the change of parameter $b$.
conclusions: the qualitative results of the paper do not change with the particular choice of the weight $b$
the extremal curves change continuously with the change of parameter $b$

nodes.name: Optimal control decreases as weight b increases
nodes.statement: We see that an increase of the value of the parameter $b$ corresponds to a decrease of the control $u$, meaning that the financial support from the Central Bank diminishes when we penalize the use of the control by increasing the value of $b$. The role of parameter $b$ is more visible in Scenario~3 than in Scenarios 1 and 2.
conclusions: an increase of the value of the parameter $b$ corresponds to a decrease of the control $u$
The role of parameter $b$ is more visible in Scenario~3 than in Scenarios 1 and 2
